★ User auditing: authorized versus unauthorized accounts, guest

Sophomore, aim: apply

Learn
  • Defense Ladder › Freshman › First look at Windows
  • Defense Ladder › Freshman › First look at Linux
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Windows 11 hardening
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Linux Mint and Ubuntu hardening
Practice
  • Defense Ladder › Freshman › First look at WindowsDrill
  • Defense Ladder › Freshman › First look at LinuxDrill
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Windows 11 hardeningDrill
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Linux Mint and Ubuntu hardeningDrill
  • Windows RangeLablook for lusrmgr
  • Linux RangeLablook for deluser
  • Windows 11 LockdownDrilllook for Get-LocalUser
  • Windows Server LockdownDrilllook for Get-LocalUser
  • Ubuntu LockdownDrilllook for deluser
  • Linux Mint LockdownDrilllook for deluser
  • FreeBSD LockdownDrilllook for rmuser
On each system
  • Windows lusrmgr.msc; Get-LocalUser; Disable-LocalUser -Name Guest; Remove-LocalUser -Name <u>
  • Linux awk -F: '$3>=1000 && $3<65534' /etc/passwd; deluser --remove-home <u>; passwd -l <u>
  • FreeBSD pw userdel <u> -r; pw lock <u>
  • Cisco IOS show running-config | include username; no username <u>
Builds on
Reading the scenario brief: authorized users and required services, Least privilege

★ Administrator rights: admin groups, sudo and wheel

Sophomore, aim: apply

Learn
  • Defense Ladder › Freshman › First look at Windows
  • Defense Ladder › Freshman › First look at Linux
  • Defense Ladder › Junior › Windows Server and Active Directory
  • Defense Ladder › Senior › FreeBSD
Practice
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Windows 11 hardeningDrill
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Linux Mint and Ubuntu hardeningDrill
  • Windows RangeLablook for Administrators
  • Linux RangeLablook for gpasswd
  • Windows 11 LockdownDrilllook for net localgroup
  • Windows Server LockdownDrilllook for net localgroup
  • Ubuntu LockdownDrilllook for gpasswd
  • Linux Mint LockdownDrilllook for gpasswd
  • FreeBSD LockdownDrilllook for wheel
Check
  • Defense Ladder › Junior › Windows Server and Active Directory (quiz)
On each system
  • Windows Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators; Remove-LocalGroupMember; domain: Domain Admins
  • Linux getent group sudo; gpasswd -d <u> sudo; visudo and /etc/sudoers.d (look for NOPASSWD)

★ Password policy: length, complexity, history, age

Sophomore, aim: apply

Learn
  • Defense Ladder › Freshman › First look at Windows
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Windows 11 hardening
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Linux Mint and Ubuntu hardening
  • Defense Ladder › Junior › Group Policy
Practice
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Windows 11 hardeningDrill
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Linux Mint and Ubuntu hardeningDrill
  • Defense Ladder › Junior › Group PolicyDrill
  • Windows RangeLablook for Minimum password length
  • Linux RangeLablook for PASS_MAX_DAYS
  • IOS CLI LabBuildMission › SSH only
  • Config AuditTroubleshootWhat's missing?
  • Windows 11 LockdownDrilllook for Minimum password length
  • Windows Server LockdownDrilllook for Minimum password length
  • Ubuntu LockdownDrilllook for PASS_MAX_DAYS
  • Linux Mint LockdownDrilllook for PASS_MAX_DAYS
  • FreeBSD LockdownDrilllook for login.conf
Check
  • Defense Ladder › Junior › Group Policy (quiz)
On each system
  • Windows secpol.msc > Account Policies > Password Policy; net accounts /minpwlen:12 /maxpwage:60 /minpwage:1 /uniquepw:24; domain: Default Domain Policy GPO
  • Linux /etc/login.defs (PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, PASS_WARN_AGE); chage -M -m -W; libpam-pwquality in /etc/pam.d/common-password
  • Cisco IOS security passwords min-length 10; enable secret and username ... secret
Builds on
Strong passwords, passphrases and multi-factor authentication

★ Account lockout

Sophomore, aim: apply

Learn
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Windows 11 hardening
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Linux Mint and Ubuntu hardening
Practice
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Windows 11 hardeningDrill
  • Windows RangeLablook for lockout
  • Linux RangeLablook for faillock

  • Linux Mint LockdownDrilllook for faillock

Learn
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Linux Mint and Ubuntu hardening
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Cisco: configure a switch and a router
Practice
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Linux Mint and Ubuntu hardeningDrill
  • Windows RangeLablook for Guest; look for Remote Desktop
  • Linux RangeLablook for PermitRootLogin; look for sshd_config
  • Cisco RangeLablook for banner motd
  • IOS CLI LabBuildMission › Lock the doors
  • Config AuditTroubleshootR1 edge router
  • Windows 11 LockdownDrilllook for Guest; look for Remote Desktop
  • Windows Server LockdownDrilllook for Guest; look for Remote Desktop
  • Ubuntu LockdownDrilllook for PermitRootLogin; look for sshd_config

Check
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Read the scenario brief first (quiz)

  • Windows no auto-login; RDP only if the scenario brief needs it, with Network Level Authentication; interactive logon options in secpol Security Options

  • Cisco IOS line vty: login local, transport input ssh, exec-timeout; banner motd

User auditing: authorized versus unauthorized accounts, guest

★ Host firewall: default deny inbound, only required ports

Sophomore, aim: apply

Learn
  • Defense Ladder › Freshman › First look at Windows
  • Defense Ladder › Freshman › First look at Linux
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Windows 11 hardening
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Linux Mint and Ubuntu hardening
  • Defense Ladder › Senior › FreeBSD
  • Defense Ladder › Junior › Debian and deeper Linux
  • Defense Ladder › Junior › Network security design: firewalls, zones, VPNs, and Wi-Fi
Practice
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Windows 11 hardeningDrill
  • Defense Ladder › Sophomore › Linux Mint and Ubuntu hardeningDrill
  • Windows RangeLablook for wf.msc
  • Linux RangeLablook for ufw
  • Windows 11 LockdownDrilllook for advfirewall
  • Windows Server LockdownDrilllook for advfirewall
  • Ubuntu LockdownDrilllook for ufw
  • Linux Mint LockdownDrilllook for ufw
  • FreeBSD LockdownDrilllook for pfctl
On each system
  • Windows wf.msc; Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain,Private,Public -Enabled True -DefaultInboundAction Block
  • Linux ufw default deny incoming; ufw allow 22/tcp (only if required); ufw enable; Debian may need nftables
  • FreeBSD /etc/pf.conf; pfctl -f /etc/pf.conf; pfctl -e; sysrc pf_enable=YES
  • Cisco IOS ACLs applied with ip access-group filter traffic through the device
Builds on
Ports and protocols

Commands

Every command in the apps, by system. The interactive page shows each one's options and where it appears.

Windows

  • $PROFILE: Shows the paths of the PowerShell profile scripts, which run every time PowerShell starts, so you can open each one and check for planted commands.
  • .\Find-ExtraAdmins.ps1: Runs Find-ExtraAdmins.ps1, the script you write in a Defense Ladder lesson, which prints enabled local administrators missing from the approved list in brief.txt.
  • Add-ADGroupMember: Adds accounts to an Active Directory group, such as putting a new staff member in the department group the brief lists.
  • Add-BitLockerKeyProtector: Adds another way to unlock a BitLocker drive, such as the 48-digit recovery password, so you can still open the drive if the usual method fails.
  • Add-LocalGroupMember: Adds a user or group to a local group, for example to give someone Remote Desktop access or administrator rights.
  • Add-MpPreference: Adds an entry to a Microsoft Defender list setting, such as turning on an attack surface reduction rule or adding an exclusion.
  • appwiz.cpl: Opens Programs and Features, the classic list of installed desktop programs, where you uninstall the ones the brief leaves out.
  • arp: Shows the ARP cache, the list matching IP addresses on your network to device MAC addresses, which helps spot ARP spoofing.
  • auditpol: Shows or sets which security events Windows records in the Security log, such as sign-ins, account changes, and new processes, for success and failure.
  • autorunsc: Lists everything set to start automatically, from Run keys and services to scheduled tasks and WMI, using the free Sysinternals Autoruns command-line tool.
  • Backup-BitLockerKeyProtector: Saves a BitLocker recovery password into Active Directory, on the computer's account, so domain admins can find it when a user is locked out.
  • BackupToAAD-BitLockerKeyProtector: Saves a BitLocker recovery password to Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD), where the user and admins can retrieve it online.
  • C:\Apache24\bin\httpd.exe: Runs the Apache web server's own program on Windows; with -t it checks the configuration files for mistakes before you restart the service.
  • cat: Prints a file's text; in PowerShell on Windows, cat is an alias for Get-Content.
  • cd: Changes the current folder; in Command Prompt, cd alone prints the folder you are in.
  • certutil: A built-in Windows tool that, among other jobs, calculates a file's hash; it is the Command Prompt twin of Get-FileHash.
  • chdir: Changes the current folder, exactly like cd.
  • clear: Clears the screen; in PowerShell, clear is an alias for Clear-Host.
  • Clear-Host: Clears the PowerShell window; cls and clear are its short aliases.
  • cls: Clears the screen of the Command Prompt or PowerShell window.
  • cmd: Opens a new Command Prompt, or with /c runs one command and closes.
  • cmdkey: Lists, adds, or deletes the usernames and passwords Windows has saved in Credential Manager for servers and websites.
  • Confirm-SecureBootUEFI: Checks whether Secure Boot is on: True means on, False means off, and an error means the PC boots in legacy BIOS mode.
  • control: Opens Control Panel, or one of its pages such as Programs and Features or System Properties.
  • curl: Fetches a web address from the command line and shows the response, which tests web servers and headers; Windows includes it as curl.exe.
  • date: Shows the date and, in Command Prompt, asks for a new one; in PowerShell, date runs Get-Date.
  • del: Deletes one or more files; with /s it searches subfolders, which removes, for example, every .mp3 under C:\Users in one command.
  • dir: Lists the files and folders in a folder, with sizes and dates.
  • Disable-ADAccount: Disables a domain account, blocking its sign-in across the domain while keeping the account for review.
  • Disable-LocalUser: Disables a local account, blocking its sign-in while keeping the account and its files for later review.
  • Disable-NetFirewallRule: Turns off a Windows Defender Firewall rule while keeping it, which is the reversible way to stop a suspicious rule.
  • Disable-ScheduledTask: Disables a scheduled task so it stops running, while keeping it for review.
  • Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature: Turns off a Windows optional feature, such as SMBv1, the Telnet Client, or the FTP server, which shrinks the attack surface.
  • dsa.msc: Opens Active Directory Users and Computers, the window for managing domain users, groups, computers, and organizational units.
  • dsregcmd: Shows how this PC is joined: to an Active Directory domain, to Microsoft Entra ID in the cloud, to both, or to neither.
  • echo: Prints text on the screen, or into a file with >; in PowerShell, echo is an alias for Write-Output.
  • Enable-ADAccount: Turns a disabled domain account back on.
  • Enable-BitLocker: Turns on BitLocker for a drive and starts encrypting it, using the protector you name, such as the TPM chip, to unlock it at startup.
  • Enable-LocalUser: Turns a disabled local account back on so it can sign in again.
  • Enable-NetFirewallRule: Turns on a Windows Defender Firewall rule that is currently off.
  • Enable-ScheduledTask: Turns a disabled scheduled task back on.
  • Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature: Turns on a Windows optional feature.
  • erase: Deletes one or more files, exactly like del.
  • eventvwr.msc: Opens Event Viewer, where you browse and filter Windows logs, such as Security sign-in events and System service events.
  • exit: Closes the current Command Prompt or PowerShell session, or ends a remote session such as SSH and returns you to your own machine.
  • Export-ScheduledTask: Prints a scheduled task's full definition as XML, its triggers, actions, and run-as account, so you can save the evidence before you delete the task.
  • findstr: Searches text files, or text piped from another command, for lines that contain a word or pattern; it is the Command Prompt twin of Select-String.
  • foreach: Repeats commands once for each item in a list, such as writing the same value into several registry settings.
  • Format-Hex: Shows a file's raw bytes in hexadecimal; every Windows program starts with the letters MZ, which exposes an .exe disguised as a PDF or picture.
  • ftp: Connects to an FTP server to move files, sending the username, password, and data as readable cleartext.
  • gc: Prints a file's text; gc is PowerShell's short alias for Get-Content.
  • gci: Lists files and folders; gci is PowerShell's short alias for Get-ChildItem and takes the same options.
  • Get-Acl: Shows a file's or folder's owner and access control list: which users and groups can read, change, or fully control it.
  • Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy: Shows the domain's password and lockout policy that every domain account follows: length, complexity, age, history, and lockout.
  • Get-ADGroupMember: Lists the members of an Active Directory group, such as Domain Admins, so you can compare privileged groups with the approved list.
  • Get-ADUser: Lists domain user accounts from Active Directory, with properties such as Enabled, PasswordNeverExpires, and group memberships, and finds accounts with risky settings.
  • Get-Alias: Lists PowerShell's short names for commands, so you can see that sc means Set-Content in Windows PowerShell 5.1 and del means Remove-Item.
  • Get-AppxPackage: Lists Microsoft Store (modern) apps installed for you or for every user, and passes them to Remove-AppxPackage to uninstall.
  • Get-AuthenticodeSignature: Checks a file's digital signature and reports whether it is Valid, NotSigned, or tampered with (HashMismatch), and who signed it.
  • Get-BitLockerVolume: Shows each drive's BitLocker state: whether it is encrypted, how far encryption has gone, whether protection is on, and which key protectors unlock it.
  • Get-ChildItem: Lists the files and folders in a location, and with -Recurse searches every folder below it, for example for media files or planted tools.
  • Get-CimInstance: Reads system information from WMI classes such as processes, services, startup items, and network adapters; it is the modern replacement for the deprecated wmic tool.
  • Get-Command: Finds commands by name or pattern, so you can discover which cmdlets exist for a job, such as everything with LocalUser in the name.
  • Get-Content: Prints the text inside a file, such as the hosts file, a config file, or a PowerShell profile; it can also read a file's hidden data streams.
  • Get-DhcpServerInDC: Lists the DHCP servers authorized in Active Directory; any other Windows DHCP server on the network is a rogue.
  • Get-DhcpServerv4Scope: Lists the IPv4 address ranges (scopes) a Windows DHCP server hands out, with their names and whether each is active.
  • Get-DnsServerResourceRecord: Lists the records in a DNS zone on a Windows DNS server, so you can look for stray or planted records.
  • Get-DnsServerZone: Lists the DNS zones a Windows DNS server hosts, with their type, dynamic-update setting, and zone-transfer setting.
  • Get-ExecutionPolicy: Shows PowerShell's script execution policy, which decides whether scripts run and whether they must be signed.
  • Get-FileHash: Calculates a file's fingerprint (SHA-256 by default), so you can compare it with a known-good value or look it up as known malware.
  • Get-GPO: Lists Group Policy Objects in the domain with their status and when each last changed, so you can spot a new or edited one.
  • Get-GPOReport: Writes a readable report of what Group Policy Objects set, as an HTML or XML file you can open in a browser.
  • Get-Help: Shows how to use a cmdlet: what it does, its parameters, and worked examples.
  • Get-History: Lists the commands typed in this PowerShell session; older sessions live in the PSReadLine history file, found with (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath.
  • Get-HotFix: Lists installed Windows updates by KB number and install date, so you can check that recent patches are in place.
  • Get-Item: Shows one file, folder, or registry key as an object; with -Stream it lists a file's hidden data streams, such as the Mark of the Web.
  • Get-ItemProperty: Reads the values stored in a registry key, such as the programs in a Run key or the UAC settings.
  • Get-LapsADPassword: Reads a computer's local administrator password that Windows LAPS rotates and stores in Active Directory, for admins who are allowed to see it.
  • Get-LocalGroup: Lists the local groups on this computer, such as Administrators, Users, and Remote Desktop Users.
  • Get-LocalGroupMember: Lists the members of a local group, most often Administrators, so you can compare them with the approved list.
  • Get-LocalUser: Lists the local user accounts on this computer with properties such as Enabled, PasswordRequired, PasswordExpires, and LastLogon.
  • Get-Location: Prints the folder PowerShell is working in right now.
  • Get-MpComputerStatus: Shows Microsoft Defender's health: whether antivirus and real-time protection are on, when signatures last updated, and whether tamper protection is on.
  • Get-MpPreference: Shows Microsoft Defender's settings, including exclusions, the folders and programs it skips, where attackers hide.
  • Get-MpThreat: Lists the threats Microsoft Defender has found on this computer, with each threat's name and whether it is still active.
  • Get-MpThreatDetection: Lists the malware Microsoft Defender has detected on this computer, with when, which program, and which account was involved.
  • Get-NetFirewallProfile: Shows the Windows Defender Firewall settings for each profile (Domain, Private, and Public): whether it is on and what it does with unmatched traffic.
  • Get-NetFirewallRule: Lists Windows Defender Firewall rules with their direction, action, and whether each is on, so you can find a rule that lets attackers in.
  • Get-NetTCPConnection: Lists TCP connections and listening ports with the owning process id, so you can trace each open port to the program behind it.
  • Get-NetUDPEndpoint: Lists the UDP ports this computer listens on, with the process id behind each, the UDP half that Get-NetTCPConnection leaves out.
  • Get-Process: Lists running processes with their ids, memory, and CPU use, and can show the program path or the account behind each one.
  • Get-ScheduledTask: Lists scheduled tasks with their folder path and state, so you can find a task that runs a planted script or re-adds a user.
  • Get-Service: Lists Windows services with their status (Running or Stopped) and start type, so you can spot risky or unknown services.
  • Get-SmbClientConfiguration: Shows this computer's SMB client settings, such as whether it requires signing and whether it allows insecure guest sign-ins to other servers.
  • Get-SmbServerConfiguration: Shows this computer's SMB file-sharing server settings, such as whether SMBv1 is on and whether signing and encryption are required.
  • Get-SmbShare: Lists the folders this computer shares over SMB, with their names and paths, so you can remove shares the brief leaves out.
  • Get-SmbShareAccess: Shows who has access to a network share and at what level: Full, Change, or Read.
  • Get-Tpm: Shows whether this PC has a TPM security chip and whether it is enabled and ready for BitLocker and Windows Hello.
  • Get-WebBinding: Lists the protocol, address, port, and host name each IIS website listens on, so you can confirm HTTPS bindings.
  • Get-WebConfigurationProperty: Reads one IIS web server setting, such as whether request logging is on or whether a site requires HTTPS, so you can confirm a change.
  • Get-Website: Lists the websites on an IIS web server with their state and the folder each one serves.
  • Get-WindowsCapability: Lists Windows capabilities, add-ons such as OpenSSH Server that install on demand, and shows which are installed.
  • Get-WindowsFeature: Lists Windows Server roles and features, such as DNS, DHCP, and Web Server, and shows which are installed.
  • Get-WindowsOptionalFeature: Lists Windows optional features, such as SMBv1, the Telnet Client, and IIS, and shows whether each is on.
  • Get-WinEvent: Searches Windows event logs, such as Security and System, for events by log name and event ID, for example failed sign-ins or new services.
  • gpedit.msc: Opens the Local Group Policy Editor, where you change computer and user policy settings, from security options to Windows Update behavior.
  • gpmc.msc: Opens Group Policy Management, where you create, edit, and link Group Policy Objects, including the Default Domain Policy that holds domain password rules.
  • gpresult: Shows which Group Policy Objects applied to this computer and user, and which were filtered out, so you can see where a setting came from.
  • gps: Lists running processes; gps is PowerShell's short alias for Get-Process.
  • gpupdate: Applies Group Policy now instead of waiting for the next refresh, which runs about every 90 minutes.
  • Grant-SmbShareAccess: Gives a user or group access to a network share at the level you choose.
  • gsv: Lists services; gsv is PowerShell's short alias for Get-Service.
  • help: Lists the built-in Command Prompt commands, or with a name shows that command's help; in PowerShell, help shows Get-Help one page at a time.
  • history: Lists the commands typed in this PowerShell session; history is an alias for Get-History.
  • hostname: Prints this computer's name.
  • icacls: Shows or changes NTFS permissions on files and folders: who can read, modify, or fully control them, and whether permissions pass down to items inside.
  • if: Runs commands only when a test is true; hardening steps use it to create a registry key with New-Item only when Test-Path finds the key missing.
  • Import-Module: Loads a PowerShell module so its cmdlets are ready to use, such as WebAdministration for IIS or ActiveDirectory for domain cmdlets.
  • Install-WindowsFeature: Installs a Windows Server role or feature, such as Microsoft Defender Antivirus after someone removed it.
  • ipconfig: Shows each network adapter's IP address, subnet mask, and default gateway; with options it shows full details, renews a DHCP address, or clears the DNS cache.
  • kill: Ends a running process; in PowerShell on Windows, kill is an alias for Stop-Process.
  • ls: Lists files and folders; in PowerShell on Windows, ls is an alias for Get-ChildItem.
  • lusrmgr.msc: Opens Local Users and Groups, a window for viewing, creating, disabling, and editing local accounts and group memberships.
  • ms-settings:windowsupdate: Opens Settings at the Windows Update page, where you check for, download, and install updates.
  • msinfo32: Opens System Information, a full report on the PC: Windows edition, BIOS mode, Secure Boot state, hardware, drivers, and running services.
  • mstsc: Opens Remote Desktop Connection, the Windows program that signs you in to another computer's desktop over RDP.
  • net accounts: Shows or sets this computer's password and lockout policy: minimum length, age, history, and lockout; on a domain, Group Policy overrides it.
  • net help: Lists the net subcommands, or with a name explains one of them.
  • net localgroup: Lists local groups, shows a group's members, or adds and removes members, for example to audit or trim the Administrators group.
  • net session: Lists the computers connected to this computer's shared folders right now, or disconnects one.
  • net share: Lists the folders this computer shares on the network, or removes a share.
  • net start: Lists the services running right now, or starts one by name.
  • net stop: Stops a running service by name.
  • net user: Lists local user accounts, shows one account's details, or creates, deletes, disables, and sets passwords for accounts.
  • netsh advfirewall firewall: Shows, adds, changes, or deletes individual Windows Defender Firewall rules from the command line.
  • netsh advfirewall reset: Puts Windows Defender Firewall back to its default settings and deletes every rule added since installation.
  • netsh advfirewall set: Turns Windows Defender Firewall on or off per profile and sets the default action for traffic no rule matches.
  • netsh advfirewall show: Shows the Windows Defender Firewall state and settings for each profile, including whether it is on and its inbound and outbound defaults.
  • netsh http show: Shows what HTTP.sys, the Windows web listener behind IIS and WinRM, serves: each web address and the process that owns it, which port lists show as System (PID 4).
  • netstat: Lists network connections and listening ports, and with options shows the process id or program behind each one.
  • New-ADGroup: Creates a group in Active Directory, such as a department group the brief lists, so you can then add its members with Add-ADGroupMember.
  • New-ADUser: Creates a user account in Active Directory, the domain's directory, such as a new staff member the brief lists.
  • New-Item: Creates a new file, folder, or registry key; hardening steps use it to create a policy key before Set-ItemProperty writes a value into it.
  • New-ItemProperty: Creates a registry value with the type you choose, or with -Force overwrites one that exists; it is the PowerShell twin of reg add.
  • New-LocalGroup: Creates a local group, such as one the brief lists for a team, so you can then add its members with Add-LocalGroupMember.
  • New-LocalUser: Creates a local user account; without -Password or -NoPassword it prompts for the password securely.
  • New-NetFirewallRule: Creates a Windows Defender Firewall rule that allows or blocks traffic, such as one port the brief requires, from just the addresses that need it.
  • notepad: Opens Notepad, the built-in text editor, optionally with a file; run it as administrator to edit system files such as the hosts file.
  • nslookup: Asks a DNS server for the address behind a name, or other records such as mail servers, and shows which server answered.
  • ping: Sends small test messages to an address or name and reports whether replies come back and how long they take.
  • powercfg: Shows or changes power plan settings; hardening uses it to require a password when the computer wakes from sleep.
  • powershell: Starts Windows PowerShell; in an investigation, flags such as -EncodedCommand, -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, or -WindowStyle Hidden in a command line signal an attacker.
  • ps: Lists running processes; in PowerShell on Windows, ps is an alias for Get-Process.
  • pwd: Prints the current folder; in PowerShell, pwd is an alias for Get-Location.
  • quser: Lists the users signed in to this computer, with each session's name, state, idle time, and sign-in time.
  • reg add: Creates or changes a registry value from the command line, used to switch security settings such as UAC, Remote Desktop, or NTLM level.
  • reg delete: Deletes a registry value, or a whole key with everything under it, from the command line.
  • reg export: Saves a registry key and its values to a .reg file, a backup to make before you change anything with reg add or reg delete.
  • reg query: Reads registry keys and values from the command line, such as UAC, Remote Desktop, or SMBv1 settings.
  • Remove-ADGroupMember: Removes an account from an Active Directory group, such as taking an unauthorized user out of Domain Admins.
  • Remove-ADUser: Deletes a domain account from Active Directory.
  • Remove-Item: Deletes files, folders, or registry keys; deleted files skip the Recycle Bin.
  • Remove-ItemProperty: Deletes one value from a registry key, such as a planted entry in a Run key that starts malware at sign-in.
  • Remove-LocalGroupMember: Removes a user or group from a local group, such as taking away administrator rights from an account that should be a standard user.
  • Remove-LocalUser: Deletes a local user account.
  • Remove-MpPreference: Removes entries from Microsoft Defender's lists, most often an exclusion an attacker added to hide a folder or program.
  • Remove-NetFirewallRule: Deletes a Windows Defender Firewall rule, such as one an attacker added to open a port.
  • Remove-SmbShare: Stops sharing a folder over the network; the folder and its files stay on disk.
  • Remove-WindowsCapability: Uninstalls a Windows capability, such as OpenSSH Server, which removes a remote-access door.
  • Remove-WindowsFeature: Removes a Windows Server role or feature; Remove-WindowsFeature is the older name of Uninstall-WindowsFeature and takes the same options.
  • Resolve-DnsName: Looks up a name in DNS and returns its records, such as its IP address or mail servers.
  • Restart-Computer: Restarts the computer.
  • Restart-Service: Stops and then starts a service, which makes it reload its settings.
  • Resume-BitLocker: Turns BitLocker protection back on for a drive after it was suspended, for example for a firmware or BIOS update.
  • Revoke-SmbShareAccess: Removes a user's or group's access to a network share, such as taking Everyone off a share meant for one team.
  • ri: Deletes files or folders; ri is PowerShell's short alias for Remove-Item.
  • rm: Deletes files or folders; in PowerShell on Windows, rm is an alias for Remove-Item.
  • rmdir: Deletes a folder; in Command Prompt it removes an empty folder (or a whole tree with /s), and in PowerShell it is an alias for Remove-Item.
  • route: Shows this computer's routing table: which gateway and interface traffic to each network leaves through.
  • runas: Runs a program as a different account; with /netonly the program keeps your identity locally and uses the other account only for network access.
  • sasv: Starts a service; sasv is PowerShell's short alias for Start-Service.
  • sc config: Changes a service's settings, most often its start type, such as disabled for an unneeded or planted service.
  • sc delete: Removes a service's registration from Windows, so a planted service is gone for good once it stops.
  • sc qc: Shows a service's configuration: its start type, program path, and the account it runs as, which reveals planted or hijackable services.
  • sc qtriggerinfo: Shows the events that start or stop a service on their own, such as a device arriving or a network request, so a Manual service can still start.
  • sc query: Shows whether services are running or stopped; alone it lists the active services.
  • sc start: Starts a service.
  • sc stop: Stops a running service.
  • schtasks: Lists, runs, disables, and deletes scheduled tasks, the programs Windows starts on a schedule or at sign-in, where attackers often hide persistence.
  • sconfig: Opens Server Configuration, a numbered text menu on Windows Server for the computer name, domain, network, Remote Desktop, and Windows Update.
  • Search-ADAccount: Finds domain accounts in a risky or notable state: inactive, locked out, disabled, expired, or with passwords that never expire.
  • secedit: Exports, applies, or compares a security template, one text file of password, lockout, user-rights, and security-option settings; it is the command-line route to password complexity.
  • secpol.msc: Opens Local Security Policy, where you set password and lockout rules, audit policy, user rights, and security options in one window.
  • Select-Object: Keeps only the properties (columns) you name from each object in the pipeline, or only the first or last few objects.
  • Select-String: Searches inside text files, or text sent down the pipeline, for lines that match a word or pattern.
  • services.msc: Opens the Services window, where you see every service and change its status, start type, and the account it runs as.
  • Set-ADAccountControl: Changes an account's security flags in Active Directory, such as requiring Kerberos pre-authentication or requiring a password.
  • Set-ADAccountPassword: Sets a new password on a domain account; with -Reset an administrator replaces it without knowing the old one.
  • Set-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy: Changes the domain-wide password and lockout policy, such as the lockout threshold, lockout duration, and minimum password length.
  • Set-ADUser: Changes a domain account's settings, such as forcing a new password at next sign-in or making its password follow expiry.
  • Set-DnsServerPrimaryZone: Changes a DNS zone's settings, such as allowing only secure dynamic updates and turning off zone transfers to unknown servers.
  • Set-ExecutionPolicy: Changes PowerShell's script execution policy, for example to RemoteSigned so your own scripts run while downloaded ones must be signed.
  • Set-ItemProperty: Writes a value into a registry key, which is how many hardening steps change Windows settings such as UAC, Remote Desktop, or credential protection.
  • Set-LocalUser: Changes a local account's settings, such as its password, whether the password expires, its full name, or its description.
  • Set-Location: Changes PowerShell's current location to a folder or another drive, including registry drives such as HKLM:.
  • Set-MpPreference: Changes Microsoft Defender's settings, such as turning real-time protection on or switching on PUA blocking, cloud protection, and controlled folder access.
  • Set-NetFirewallProfile: Turns Windows Defender Firewall on or off for each profile and sets what happens to traffic that matches no rule.
  • Set-NetFirewallRule: Changes an existing Windows Defender Firewall rule, for example so Remote Desktop accepts connections only from the admin subnet.
  • Set-Service: Changes a service's start type, for example to Disabled so an unneeded service stays off after a restart.
  • Set-SmbClientConfiguration: Changes this computer's SMB client settings, such as requiring signing when it connects to file servers.
  • Set-SmbServerConfiguration: Changes this computer's SMB file-sharing server settings, such as turning SMBv1 off or requiring signing and encryption.
  • Set-WebConfigurationProperty: Changes an IIS configuration setting, such as turning off directory browsing, which hides a site's file list from visitors.
  • shell:common startup: Opens the all-users Startup folder (type shell:common startup), whose shortcuts and files run when anyone signs in.
  • shell:startup: Opens your own Startup folder, which holds shortcuts and files that run every time you sign in.
  • shutdown: Shuts down, restarts, or signs out of the computer, now or after a delay, and can cancel a pending shutdown.
  • sl: Changes the current location; sl is PowerShell's short alias for Set-Location.
  • spps: Ends a running process; spps is PowerShell's short alias for Stop-Process.
  • spsv: Stops a service; spsv is PowerShell's short alias for Stop-Service.
  • ssh: Opens an encrypted remote session on another device, such as a switch or server, using the OpenSSH client built into Windows.
  • Start-MpScan: Starts a Microsoft Defender malware scan: quick, full, or of one folder.
  • Start-Service: Starts a stopped Windows service.
  • Stop-Computer: Shuts the computer down.
  • Stop-Process: Ends a running process by its id or name; disable the service or task that starts it first, or it comes back.
  • Stop-Service: Stops a running Windows service until it is started again or the computer restarts.
  • systeminfo: Prints a summary of the computer: Windows edition and build, install date, last boot time, domain, installed updates, and network cards.
  • SystemPropertiesRemote: Opens System Properties on the Remote tab, where you turn Remote Assistance and Remote Desktop on or off and require Network Level Authentication.
  • tar: Lists or unpacks the files inside an archive; with -tf it shows what a .zip holds without extracting or running anything.
  • taskkill: Ends a running process by its process id or program name.
  • tasklist: Lists running processes with their process ids and memory use, and can show the services each process hosts.
  • taskschd.msc: Opens Task Scheduler, the window that shows every task set to run on a schedule or at sign-in, with its triggers and actions.
  • telnet: Opens an unencrypted remote session or tests whether a TCP port answers; Windows 11 includes the Telnet Client as an optional feature that is off by default.
  • Test-NetConnection: Tests whether a host answers and whether a TCP port on it accepts connections, which works even when ping is blocked.
  • Test-Path: Answers True or False: does this file, folder, or registry key exist, so a step creates a policy key only when it is missing.
  • time: Shows the current time and asks for a new one; press Enter to keep it.
  • tpm.msc: Opens TPM Management, which shows the TPM chip's status and its specification version (Windows 11 needs 2.0).
  • tracert: Lists each router on the path to a destination, which shows where traffic stops along the way.
  • type: Prints the text inside a file; in PowerShell, type is an alias for Get-Content.
  • Unblock-File: Removes the Mark of the Web from a downloaded file, which lifts the warnings and script blocks Windows applies to internet files.
  • Uninstall-WindowsFeature: Removes a Windows Server role or feature, such as the FTP server, SMBv1, or the Telnet Client, which shrinks the attack surface.
  • Unlock-ADAccount: Unlocks a domain account that the lockout policy locked after too many failed sign-ins.
  • Unregister-ScheduledTask: Deletes a scheduled task.
  • Update-MpSignature: Downloads the newest Microsoft Defender signatures, so it recognizes the latest malware.
  • UserAccountControlSettings: Opens the User Account Control slider, where Always notify is the top position and the default sits one step below it.
  • ver: Prints the Windows version and build number; Windows 11 still reports itself as version 10.0 with a build of 22000 or higher.
  • w32tm: Shows and configures the Windows Time service, which keeps the clock in sync; domain sign-in fails when clocks drift more than five minutes apart.
  • wbadmin: Makes and manages built-in Windows image backups, including everything needed to restore the whole machine onto a blank disk.
  • wevtutil epl: Exports an event log to an .evtx file, so you can save evidence before it is overwritten and open it on another machine.
  • wevtutil sl: Changes an event log's settings, such as its maximum size, or turns on a log that ships switched off, such as Task Scheduler history.
  • wf.msc: Opens Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security, the window for profiles, inbound and outbound rules, and firewall logging.
  • Where-Object: Keeps only the objects in the pipeline that pass a test, such as accounts whose Enabled property is True.
  • whoami: Shows which account you are using right now, and with options lists your groups, privileges, and security identifier (SID).
  • windowsdefender:: Opens the Windows Security app, where you check virus and threat protection, the firewall, and device security.
  • winget list: Lists the apps installed on this computer, including desktop programs and Store apps, with their versions.
  • winget uninstall: Removes an installed app by name or id, such as a hacking tool or game the brief leaves out.
  • winget upgrade: Lists the apps with a newer version available, or updates one app or every app, including desktop programs such as browsers.
  • winrm: Shows or changes the settings of WinRM, the service behind PowerShell remoting, such as whether it accepts Basic sign-in or unencrypted traffic.
  • winver: Opens the About Windows box, which shows the edition, the version (such as 24H2), and the OS build number.
  • Write-Output: Sends text or objects down the pipeline, which prints them on screen when nothing else receives them; scripts use it to report results.
  • wt: Opens Windows Terminal, the Windows 11 app that holds PowerShell, Command Prompt, and other shells in tabs.

Linux

  • ./audit_users.sh: Runs the lesson's own Bash audit script from the current folder, which lists the human accounts and flags any name the scenario brief leaves out.
  • ./set_aging.sh: The example script from the Defense Ladder's scripting unit: it backs up /etc/login.defs, sets each password-aging key with sed, and greps each one as proof.
  • a2disconf: Turns off an Apache settings file by removing its link from conf-enabled; reload Apache to apply it.
  • a2enconf: Turns on an Apache settings file by linking it from conf-available into conf-enabled; reload Apache to apply it.
  • a2query: Reports whether an Apache module, settings file, or site is turned on.
  • aa-enforce: Switches an AppArmor profile to enforce mode, so the program it covers is blocked from anything the profile leaves out.
  • aa-logprof: Reads AppArmor's logged denials and complain-mode events and offers new profile rules for each, one question at a time.
  • aa-status: Shows whether AppArmor is on, how many profiles are loaded, which are in enforce or complain mode, and which running processes they confine.
  • add-apt-repository: Adds a software repository or PPA to apt's sources, or takes one away with --remove.
  • addgroup: Creates a new group with Debian's friendlier front end to groupadd; adduser or gpasswd then adds its members.
  • adduser: Creates a user with a home folder and asks for a password and details; with two names, adds an existing user to a group.
  • aide: Compares every watched file against the AIDE database and lists each file added, removed, or changed since the database was built.
  • aideinit: Builds the first AIDE database: a known-good record of file hashes that later checks compare against, so build it after hardening.
  • alias: Lists the shell's command shortcuts, or makes a new one that runs a longer command when you type a short name.
  • apache2: The Apache web server program; you start, stop, and check it with systemctl apache2 rather than by typing its name.
  • apache2ctl: Controls the Apache web server; configtest checks every settings file for mistakes before you reload.
  • apachectl: Another name for apache2ctl; configtest checks Apache's settings before you reload the web server.
  • apt autoclean: Deletes downloaded package files that can no longer be downloaded, such as old versions, freeing disk space.
  • apt autopurge: Removes packages that were installed only as dependencies and are now unused, along with their configuration files.
  • apt autoremove: Removes packages that were installed only as dependencies and are now unused.
  • apt clean: Empties apt's download cache in /var/cache/apt/archives, freeing disk space.
  • apt dist-upgrade: Upgrades every package and adds or removes packages when needed to finish; the older name for apt full-upgrade.
  • apt full-upgrade: Upgrades every package and adds or removes packages when needed to finish the upgrade.
  • apt install: Downloads and installs packages, and anything they need, from the system's trusted repositories.
  • apt list: Lists packages: everything installed, everything with a newer version waiting, or the names matching a pattern.
  • apt policy: Lists every repository apt uses with its priority; with a package name, shows the installed and candidate versions and where each comes from.
  • apt purge: Removes packages along with their system-wide configuration files.
  • apt remove: Uninstalls packages but keeps their system-wide configuration files.
  • apt search: Searches package names and descriptions in the repositories for a word or pattern.
  • apt show: Shows a package's details: version, size, dependencies, source, and description.
  • apt update: Downloads fresh package lists from every repository, so apt knows the newest versions; it installs nothing.
  • apt upgrade: Installs the newer version of every installed package, the kernel included, keeping all packages already present.
  • apt-cache: Reads apt's package lists: searches them, shows one package's details, or shows its version and source.
  • apt-config: Prints the apt settings in force after every file in /etc/apt/apt.conf.d is read, so a later file that turns automatic updates off shows up.
  • apt-get install: Installs packages from the trusted repositories; the older apt-get form that scripts use.
  • apt-key: Lists or removes keys in apt's old shared keyring; deprecated, since current releases keep each repository's key in /etc/apt/keyrings.
  • apt-mark: Marks packages as held, so updates skip them, or as installed by hand or automatically, and lists each group.
  • arp: Shows the ARP cache: the IP addresses on your local network and the MAC addresses they answered with.
  • atq: Lists one-time jobs queued with at, with job numbers and run times (sudo shows every user's); on stock Ubuntu, which ships without at, command not found means no jobs exist.
  • atrm: Deletes a queued at job by its job number.
  • audit2allow: Turns SELinux denials from the audit log into allow rules you can review and load; the SELinux partner of aa-logprof.
  • auditctl: Controls the kernel's audit system: lists the loaded rules, shows its status, and adds a watch that logs who touches a file.
  • augenrules: Merges the rule files in /etc/audit/rules.d into /etc/audit/audit.rules; with --load it also loads them into the kernel.
  • aureport: Builds summary reports from the audit log, such as which programs ran, sign-ins, and authentication attempts.
  • ausearch: Searches the audit log for events by rule key, message type, or user, answering questions like who changed /etc/passwd and when.
  • avahi-daemon: The service program that announces and finds devices on the local network (mDNS); you manage it with systemctl.
  • awk: Splits each line into fields and prints or tests them, such as listing every account whose user ID is 0.
  • base64: Encodes text or a file as base64, or with -d decodes base64 back to the original, which unmasks hidden commands.
  • bash: Starts the Bash shell or runs a script file with it, which works even where the file lacks execute permission.
  • builtin: Runs the shell's own built-in version of a command, skipping any function or alias with the same name.
  • cat: Prints a file's whole contents to the screen, or joins several files into one stream.
  • cd: Changes the folder you are working in.
  • chage: Shows or sets one account's password aging: how long a password lasts, how soon it can change, the warning, and expiry.
  • chattr: Sets or clears special file attributes, such as immutable, which blocks every change to a file, even by root.
  • chgrp: Changes which group owns a file or folder.
  • chkrootkit: Scans for signs of known rootkits, such as replaced system programs and hidden files.
  • chmod: Changes who can read, write, or run a file, with numbers such as 640 or symbols such as g-w or u-s.
  • chown: Changes the user and group that own a file or folder, such as root:shadow for /etc/shadow.
  • chpasswd: Sets passwords for many accounts at once from lines of user:password typed or piped in.
  • chronyc: Shows how closely the clock follows its time servers when chrony is the time service; Ubuntu 24.04 and Mint 22 use timesyncd until you install chrony.
  • clamscan: Scans files and folders for known malware with ClamAV's signatures.
  • clear: Clears the terminal screen.
  • command: Runs a program while skipping any shell function or alias of that name; command -v prints what a name runs.
  • cp: Copies files or folders; with -a it keeps owner, mode, and times, which makes a safe backup before an edit.
  • cron: The service program that runs scheduled jobs from crontabs and /etc/cron.d; you manage it with systemctl.
  • crontab: Lists, edits, or removes a user's scheduled cron jobs; with sudo it handles root's or another user's.
  • cupsd: The CUPS printing service program; you manage it with systemctl cups.
  • curl: Sends a web request and prints or saves the answer; -sI shows only the response headers.
  • cut: Keeps chosen fields or characters from each line, such as the name and UID columns of /etc/passwd.
  • date: Prints the current date and time, in any format you choose.
  • dd: Copies raw data block by block, such as imaging a whole evidence disk into a file.
  • debsums: Checks installed package files against the hashes their packages shipped with and lists any that changed.
  • delgroup: Deletes a group; with --only-if-empty it deletes the group only when no user still belongs to it.
  • deluser: Deletes a user account, or with a user and a group, removes that user from the group, such as sudo.
  • df: Shows each mounted disk's size, used space, and free space.
  • diff: Compares two files line by line and prints only what differs, so you can prove exactly what an edit changed.
  • dig: Asks a DNS server a question and shows the full answer, such as a name's address or an address's name.
  • dir: Lists a folder's contents in columns, like ls.
  • dmesg: Prints the kernel's message buffer: hardware events, driver messages, and crashes such as repeated segfaults.
  • docker: Manages containers; docker inspect prints a container's full settings, such as whether it runs privileged, as root, or with host folders mounted.
  • dpkg: The low-level package tool: lists installed packages, names the package that owns a file, and shows a package's files and status.
  • dpkg-query: Reads the installed-package database, such as listing every installed package with its version.
  • dpkg-reconfigure: Asks an installed package's setup questions again, such as turning automatic security updates on for unattended-upgrades.
  • echo: Prints text, with variables filled in; scripts use it for messages and to feed text into other commands.
  • egrep: The old name for grep -E (extended patterns); current grep still runs it but prints a warning to use grep -E.
  • env: Prints every environment variable, or runs a command with changed variables.
  • exit: Closes the current shell, ending a root shell, an SSH session, or the terminal.
  • export: Sets a shell variable and passes it to every program started from this shell.
  • faillock: Shows an account's recent failed sign-ins counted by pam_faillock, or resets the count to unlock it.
  • false: Does nothing and ends with exit code 1 (failure); /bin/false as a login shell blocks sign-in.
  • fgrep: The old name for grep -F (fixed text, no patterns); current grep still runs it but prints a warning to use grep -F.
  • file: Names a file's real type by reading its first bytes, whatever its extension claims.
  • find: Searches folders for files by name, type, permissions, owner, or date, and can run a command on each one it finds.
  • findmnt: Shows mounted filesystems as a tree with their mount options, such as whether /tmp has noexec.
  • firefox: Opens the Firefox web browser, optionally at a web address.
  • flatpak list: Lists the apps and runtimes installed through Flatpak, which apt list leaves out.
  • flatpak remotes: Lists the repositories (remotes) Flatpak installs from, such as flathub.
  • flatpak uninstall: Removes an app installed through Flatpak, by its application ID.
  • flatpak update: Updates every installed Flatpak app and runtime, which apt upgrade leaves out.
  • for: Repeats commands once for each item in a list, such as every account name in /etc/passwd.
  • free: Shows how much memory and swap is in use and how much is free.
  • freshclam: Downloads the newest ClamAV malware signatures.
  • gdm3: The GNOME sign-in screen (display manager) program; its auto-login settings live in /etc/gdm3/custom.conf.
  • getcap: Lists files that carry Linux capabilities, a piece of root power such as binding low ports or reading any file.
  • getenforce: Prints SELinux's mode: Enforcing, Permissive, or Disabled; Ubuntu and Mint use AppArmor instead.
  • getent: Looks up entries in the system's account databases, such as who belongs to the sudo group or one account's line.
  • getfacl: Lists a file's access control list: the extra user and group permissions a + after the mode hints at.
  • gnome-terminal: Opens a new GNOME Terminal window.
  • gnome-text-editor: Opens a file in GNOME's graphical text editor.
  • gpasswd: Manages one group's members: adds a user, removes a user, or sets the whole member list.
  • grep: Prints the lines of files or command output that match a pattern, such as every failed password in auth.log.
  • groupadd: Creates a new group.
  • groupdel: Deletes a group.
  • groups: Lists the groups a user belongs to.
  • grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2: Turns a password you type into a PBKDF2 hash for the GRUB boot menu's superuser setting.
  • gsettings: Reads or changes desktop settings for the current user, such as turning on the screen lock and the idle delay.
  • halt: Stops the operating system and leaves the machine on at a halted screen; poweroff also cuts the power.
  • hash: Lists or clears the shell's memory of where each command's program lives.
  • head: Prints the first lines of a file or of command output, ten unless you choose.
  • help: Lists Bash's built-in commands, or explains one, such as help cd.
  • history: Lists the commands typed in this shell, numbered, which makes a handy change log.
  • hostname: Prints the machine's name, or its IP addresses with -I.
  • hostnamectl hostname: Prints the machine's name, or with a name sets it permanently.
  • hostnamectl set-hostname: Sets the machine's name permanently.
  • iconv: Converts text from one character encoding to another, such as decoding UTF-16LE text from an encoded PowerShell command.
  • id: Prints a user's ID number, main group, and every group they belong to.
  • ifconfig: Shows each network interface's addresses; the older net-tools command that ip addr replaces.
  • inetd: The old super-server that starts services such as telnet when a connection arrives; you manage it with systemctl.
  • ip addr: Shows the IP addresses on every network interface, or adds one.
  • ip link: Lists the network interfaces with their state (UP or DOWN) and MAC addresses.
  • ip neigh: Shows the neighbor (ARP) cache: local IP addresses, their MAC addresses, and whether each is REACHABLE or STALE.
  • ip route: Shows the routing table: the default gateway and which interface each network is reached through.
  • ip6tables: Lists the kernel's IPv6 firewall rules, the half of the stack ufw leaves open when its IPv6 setting is off.
  • iptables: Lists the firewall rules actually loaded in the kernel, including ones in /etc/ufw/before.rules that ufw status leaves out.
  • journalctl: Reads the systemd journal: every service's log messages, filtered by service, time, boot, or priority.
  • jq: Reads JSON and prints the fields you ask for, such as every IP address with 20 or more failures.
  • kill: Sends a signal to a process by its ID number, normally to end it.
  • killall: Ends every process with an exact program name.
  • last: Lists recent sign-ins and reboots, newest first, with where each came from and how long it lasted.
  • lastb: Lists recent failed sign-in attempts, newest first.
  • lastlog: Lists every account with the time and place of its most recent sign-in, or Never logged in.
  • less: Shows a file one screen at a time, so you can scroll and search it without running or changing anything; q quits.
  • lightdm: The LightDM sign-in screen (display manager) program; its guest and auto-login settings live in /etc/lightdm.
  • ln: Makes a link: a second name for a file, or with -s a shortcut that leads to a path.
  • locate: Finds files by name in seconds by searching an index that updatedb builds, rather than the disk itself; the index leaves out /tmp, /var/spool, /media, and memory filesystems such as /dev/shm.
  • logger: Writes a message into the system log, so a script's results land somewhere trusted.
  • loginctl disable-linger: Turns off lingering for a user, so systemd stops that user's own service manager and its services once their last session ends.
  • loginctl enable-linger: Turns on lingering for a user, so their own systemd services start at boot and keep running after they sign out; disable-linger turns it back off.
  • loginctl kill-user: Sends a signal to every process of one user, ending them all by default; terminate-user also closes the user's sessions.
  • loginctl list-sessions: Lists the open sign-in sessions with their session ID, user, seat, and terminal; bare loginctl prints the same list.
  • loginctl list-users: Lists the users that have a session open or lingering turned on, with their user ID and whether each one lingers.
  • loginctl terminate-user: Ends every session of one user and the processes inside them, so a removed group or a locked account takes effect at once.
  • logout: Ends a login shell, such as an SSH session or a console sign-in.
  • ls: Lists a folder's contents; -l adds permissions, owner, size, and date, and -a includes hidden files.
  • lsattr: Lists files' special attributes; an i in the list means immutable, which blocks every change, even by root.
  • lsb_release: Prints the distribution's name, release number, and code name.
  • lsblk: Lists disks and their partitions as a tree with sizes and mount places; -f adds filesystem types such as crypto_LUKS.
  • lslogins: Lists every account with its UID, last sign-in, and password state; it also works where lastlog is missing.
  • lsof: Lists open files, including network connections, with the process that holds each one.
  • lynis: Audits the system's security settings and writes warnings, suggestions, and a hardening index to /var/log/lynis-report.dat, changing nothing.
  • man: Opens the manual page for a command, listing every option it takes; q quits and / searches.
  • mawk: A fast version of awk, the one Ubuntu and Mint install as awk; it splits lines into fields and prints or tests them.
  • md5sum: Prints a file's MD5 hash; fine for spotting accidental change, but SHA-256 is the choice when tampering matters.
  • mintupdate-automation: Linux Mint only: turns automatic updates on or off, the same switch as Update Manager's Automation tab.
  • mintupdate-cli: Linux Mint only: lists or installs the updates Update Manager offers, from the command line.
  • mkdir: Creates a folder; -p also creates any missing parent folders.
  • mokutil: Manages Secure Boot's Machine Owner Keys; --sb-state prints whether Secure Boot is on.
  • more: Shows a file one screen at a time; space goes forward and q quits.
  • mv: Moves or renames files and folders.
  • mysql: Opens the MySQL command-line client; with -e it runs one SQL statement and exits, such as listing the database accounts.
  • mysql_secure_installation: Runs MySQL's hardening wizard: sets root's sign-in, removes anonymous users and the test database, and blocks remote root sign-in.
  • mysqld: The MySQL database server program; you manage it with systemctl mysql.
  • nano: Opens a file in the nano text editor; Ctrl+O saves, Ctrl+X exits, and Ctrl+W searches.
  • nautilus: Opens a folder in Files, the GNOME file manager used on Ubuntu.
  • nc: Netcat: opens a raw network connection; nc -zv tests whether a port answers.
  • nemo: Opens a folder in Nemo, the Linux Mint file manager.
  • netstat: Lists network connections and listening ports; the older net-tools command that ss replaces.
  • NetworkManager: The service program that brings up wired and Wi-Fi connections; you manage it with systemctl and nmcli rather than typing its name.
  • nft: Manages nftables, the kernel firewall under ufw; nft list ruleset prints every rule actually loaded.
  • nginx: The nginx web server program; nginx -t tests its settings before a reload, and nginx -T prints the whole configuration in force.
  • nice: Starts a command at a lower (or, with sudo, higher) scheduling priority.
  • nmap: Scans machines for open ports and the services behind them; scan only your own lab or with permission.
  • nmbd: Samba's NetBIOS name service program; you manage it with systemctl nmbd.
  • nmcli connection: Lists and manages NetworkManager's saved connections, such as every Wi-Fi network the machine remembers.
  • nohup: Runs a command that keeps going after you sign out, writing its output to nohup.out.
  • npm: Node.js's package manager; npm audit lists known vulnerabilities in a project's dependencies.
  • openssl: A toolkit for certificates and encryption: x509 reads a certificate, dgst hashes a file, and s_client tests a TLS server.
  • pam-auth-update: Rebuilds the shared PAM files in /etc/pam.d, such as common-auth, from the profiles in /usr/share/pam-configs, turning modules such as pam_faillock on or off.
  • passwd: Changes a password, or for an administrator locks, unlocks, expires, or shows the state of any account's password.
  • perl: Runs a Perl script or a one-line Perl program.
  • pgrep: Prints the process IDs of programs whose names match a pattern.
  • pidof: Prints the process IDs of a program by its exact name.
  • ping: Sends echo requests to a machine and shows whether and how fast it answers; on Linux it runs until Ctrl+C.
  • pip-audit: Checks a Python project's installed packages against known vulnerabilities.
  • pkill: Ends processes whose names match a pattern.
  • plocate: The program behind locate on Ubuntu and Mint: finds files by name in the index updatedb builds; plocate and locate take the same options.
  • poweroff: Shuts the system down and turns the power off.
  • printenv: Prints every environment variable, or the value of one.
  • printf: Prints text in a format you set, such as padded columns or a value on each line.
  • ps: Lists running processes with their IDs, users, and commands.
  • pstree: Draws running processes as a tree, showing which program started which.
  • pwd: Prints the full path of the folder you are in.
  • python3: Runs a Python script or a short Python command, such as decoding URL-encoded text or checking a JSON file.
  • reboot: Restarts the system.
  • resolvectl status: Shows the DNS servers and search domains the system uses, overall and for each interface.
  • rgrep: Searches every file under a folder for a pattern; the same as grep -r.
  • rkhunter: Rootkit Hunter: checks for known rootkit files, changed system programs, and suspicious settings.
  • rm: Deletes files, or with -r whole folders, skipping the trash.
  • rmdir: Deletes empty folders.
  • rnano: Restricted nano: edits only the file named, and blocks opening others or saving under a new name.
  • rsync: Copies files and folders, sending only what changed, which makes it good for backups.
  • rsyslogd: The system logging program that writes /var/log/syslog and /var/log/auth.log; you manage it with systemctl rsyslog.
  • rvim: Restricted Vim: edits files but blocks running shell commands from inside the editor.
  • scp: Copies files to or from another machine over SSH.
  • sed: Edits text line by line with a script; sed -i changes a file in place, such as setting PermitRootLogin no.
  • service: The older way to start, stop, or check a service; on Ubuntu and Mint it passes the request to systemctl.
  • set: Turns shell options on or off; scripts use set -euo pipefail to stop at the first error or unset variable.
  • setfacl: Adds, changes, or removes extra user and group permissions in a file's access control list.
  • sftp: Opens an interactive file transfer session to another machine over SSH.
  • sha1sum: Prints a file's SHA-1 hash, 40 hex characters long, or checks files against a saved list; use it when a question names SHA-1, and SHA-256 when tampering matters.
  • sha256sum: Prints a file's SHA-256 hash, or checks files against a saved list of hashes to find any that changed.
  • sha512sum: Prints a file's SHA-512 hash, 128 hex characters long, or checks files against a saved list of hashes.
  • shopt: Lists or changes Bash's extra shell options.
  • shutdown: Powers off or restarts the system now or after a delay, warning signed-in users first.
  • sleep: Waits the given number of seconds, often between steps in a script.
  • smbd: The Samba file-sharing server program; you manage it with systemctl smbd.
  • snap list: Lists the apps installed as snaps, which apt list leaves out.
  • snap refresh: Updates every installed snap to its newest version now; a snap whose app is still open, such as Firefox, refuses until the app closes.
  • snap remove: Uninstalls a snap app.
  • sort: Sorts lines alphabetically or by number; sort | uniq -c | sort -rn ranks repeats, busiest first.
  • source: Runs a file's commands in the current shell, such as reloading ~/.bashrc after an edit.
  • ss: Lists network sockets: which ports are listening, which connections are open, and with sudo, which program owns each.
  • ssh: Signs in to another machine's shell over an encrypted connection.
  • ssh-copy-id: Adds your public key to a remote account's authorized_keys, so you can sign in with the key.
  • ssh-keygen: Makes an SSH key pair, or reads a key's fingerprint.
  • sshd: The SSH server program; sshd -t checks sshd_config for mistakes and sshd -T prints the settings actually in force.
  • stat: Shows a file's full details: size, permissions, owner, and its access, modify, change, and birth times.
  • strings: Prints the readable text hidden in a binary file, such as names, addresses, and commands inside a program or document.
  • su: Switches to another account, root by default, after that account's password.
  • sudo: Runs a command as root or another user after asking your own password; sudo -l lists what an account may run, exposing broad rules such as NOPASSWD: ALL.
  • sudoedit: Edits a protected file safely: you edit a copy as yourself and sudo writes it back, so a sudoers rule can allow one file only.
  • sysctl: Reads or changes kernel settings while the system runs, such as turning off IP forwarding or loading hardening files.
  • systemctl cat: Prints a service's unit file plus every drop-in override, which can quietly replace the program it runs.
  • systemctl daemon-reexec: Restarts systemd itself in place, keeping every service running; used after systemd is upgraded.
  • systemctl daemon-reload: Rereads every unit file after you add, edit, or delete one, so systemd uses the current versions.
  • systemctl disable: Stops a service from starting at boot; with --now it also stops it right away.
  • systemctl edit: Opens an override file for a service, so you can add settings such as sandboxing without changing the original unit.
  • systemctl enable: Sets a service to start at every boot; with --now it also starts it right away.
  • systemctl halt: Stops the operating system and leaves the machine on at a halted screen.
  • systemctl is-active: Prints one word for a service: active when it runs now, otherwise inactive or failed.
  • systemctl is-enabled: Prints whether a service starts at boot: enabled, disabled, masked, or static.
  • systemctl is-failed: Prints whether a service has failed: failed, or its current state.
  • systemctl list-sockets: Lists the sockets systemd listens on for other units, with the address and the service each one starts, such as ssh.socket on port 22.
  • systemctl list-timers: Lists systemd timers, the second scheduler beside cron, with when each last ran and runs next.
  • systemctl list-unit-files: Lists every installed unit with its boot setting, such as every service set to start at boot.
  • systemctl list-units: Lists the units systemd has loaded with their state, such as every service running now.
  • systemctl mask: Blocks a unit from starting at all, even by hand or as another unit's dependency, by linking it to /dev/null.
  • systemctl poweroff: Shuts the system down and turns the power off.
  • systemctl reboot: Restarts the system.
  • systemctl reload: Tells a running service to reread its settings while it keeps running, so open sessions stay connected.
  • systemctl reload-or-restart: Reloads a service's settings when it supports that, and otherwise restarts it.
  • systemctl restart: Stops and starts a service, so it runs with its current settings.
  • systemctl start: Starts a service now; it changes nothing about boot.
  • systemctl status: Shows a service's state, whether it starts at boot, its unit file, its main process, and its latest log lines.
  • systemctl stop: Stops a service now; it may start again at boot unless you also disable it.
  • systemctl try-restart: Restarts a service only if it is already running.
  • systemctl unmask: Removes a mask, so the unit can be started and enabled again.
  • systemd-analyze: Analyzes systemd; systemd-analyze security rates how exposed a service is, from 10 (unrestricted) down toward 0 (tightly sandboxed).
  • systemd-cryptenroll: Adds a way to unlock an encrypted LUKS disk, such as a TPM chip, so an unattended reboot unlocks it.
  • tail: Prints the last lines of a file, ten unless you choose; -f keeps printing new lines as a log grows.
  • tar: Packs files into a .tar archive or unpacks one; tar -tvf lists the contents without unpacking.
  • tcpdump: Captures network packets and prints them, or saves them to a file for Wireshark.
  • tee: Copies its input to the screen and into a file; sudo tee writes a file only root can write.
  • telnetd: The Telnet server program, which sends passwords in plain text on port 23; remove it unless the brief requires it.
  • test: Checks a condition, such as whether a file exists or two strings match, and sets the exit code; scripts write it as [ ].
  • testparm: Checks Samba's smb.conf for mistakes and prints the settings Samba will actually use.
  • time: Runs a command and then reports how long it took.
  • timedatectl: Shows the clock, time zone, and whether the clock syncs with a time server; it can also change them.
  • timedatectl set-ntp: Turns network time sync on or off, so the clock keeps matching a time server.
  • timedatectl status: Shows the local and UTC time, the time zone, and whether the clock is synchronized.
  • timeshift: Takes or restores system snapshots, so you can roll the system back after a bad change; home folders stay out by default.
  • top: Shows a live, updating list of processes ranked by CPU use, with memory and load; q quits.
  • touch: Creates an empty file, or updates an existing file's timestamps.
  • tr: Swaps, squeezes, or deletes characters, such as turning the null separators in /proc/<pid>/cmdline into spaces.
  • traceroute: Lists each router on the path to a destination, with how long each hop takes to answer.
  • true: Does nothing and ends with exit code 0 (success).
  • type: Tells what a name runs when you type it: an alias, a shell function, a built-in, or a program file.
  • ufw allow: Adds a firewall rule that lets traffic in to a port, service, or app, optionally only from one address.
  • ufw default: Sets what the firewall does with traffic no rule matches, such as deny incoming and allow outgoing.
  • ufw delete: Removes a firewall rule, by its number from ufw status numbered or by repeating the rule.
  • ufw deny: Adds a firewall rule that silently drops traffic to a port, service, or app.
  • ufw disable: Turns the ufw firewall off now and at boot.
  • ufw enable: Turns the ufw firewall on now and at every boot.
  • ufw limit: Allows a port but blocks an address that opens six or more connections in 30 seconds, slowing password guessing.
  • ufw logging: Turns firewall logging on or off, or sets how much it records, into /var/log/ufw.log.
  • ufw reject: Adds a firewall rule that refuses traffic and tells the sender, instead of dropping it silently.
  • ufw reload: Reloads the firewall so edits to its rule files take effect.
  • ufw show: Prints firewall reports, such as every rule ufw loads into the kernel, including ones from before.rules.
  • ufw status: Shows whether the ufw firewall is active and lists its rules; verbose adds the defaults and logging level.
  • ufw version: Prints the installed ufw version.
  • ulimit: Shows or sets this shell's resource limits, such as open files and core dump size.
  • umask: Shows or sets this shell's mask that decides new files' default permissions, such as 027; sign-in sessions start from UMASK in /etc/login.defs.
  • unalias: Removes a shell alias, such as a planted one on sudo.
  • uname: Prints system facts: the kernel name and version, the machine name, and the hardware type.
  • unattended-upgrade: Installs pending security updates now, the same job the automatic updates run on their timer.
  • unattended-upgrades: Another name for unattended-upgrade: installs pending security updates now.
  • uniq: Merges repeated neighboring lines into one; -c adds how many times each appeared, so sort first.
  • unset: Removes a shell variable or function.
  • unzip: Unpacks a .zip archive; unzip -l lists the files inside without unpacking anything.
  • update-grub: Rebuilds GRUB's boot menu file from /etc/default/grub, the drop-ins in /etc/default/grub.d, and the scripts in /etc/grub.d; kernel options such as audit=1 apply at the next boot.
  • update-rc.d: Sets whether an older-style /etc/init.d service starts at boot; on systemd systems systemctl enable and disable do this.
  • updatedb: Rebuilds the file-name index that locate searches, so files made since the last daily update show up.
  • updatedb.plocate: The program behind updatedb on Ubuntu and Mint: rebuilds the file-name index that locate searches, so files made since the last daily update show up.
  • uptime: Prints how long the system has run since its last boot, how many users are signed in, and the load.
  • useradd: Creates a user account with exactly the options you give; unlike adduser, it adds a home folder only with -m.
  • userdel: Deletes a user account; -r also removes its home folder and mail.
  • usermod: Changes an existing account: adds it to groups, locks or unlocks it, or changes its shell, name, or home.
  • users: Prints the names of everyone signed in now, on one line.
  • vdir: Lists a folder's contents in long form, like ls -l.
  • vi: Opens a file in the vi editor: i starts typing, Esc stops, :wq saves and quits, and :q! quits without saving.
  • vigr: Opens /etc/group in an editor and locks the file against other tools during the edit; vigr -s opens /etc/gshadow.
  • vim: Opens a file in the Vim editor: i starts typing, Esc stops, :wq saves and quits, and :q! quits without saving.
  • vim.tiny: A small build of Vim that Ubuntu and Mint install as vi; it edits files with the same keys.
  • vimdiff: Opens two or more files side by side in Vim with their differences highlighted.
  • vipw: Opens /etc/passwd in an editor and locks the file against other tools during the edit; vipw -s opens /etc/shadow.
  • visudo: Edits the sudoers file safely: it locks the file and checks the syntax before saving, so a typo cannot break sudo.
  • vsftpd: The vsftpd FTP server program; you manage it with systemctl vsftpd, or remove it when the brief leaves FTP out.
  • w: Shows who is signed in, from where, since when, and what each person is running now.
  • watch: Runs a command again and again, every two seconds by default, showing the latest output full screen.
  • wc: Counts the lines, words, and bytes in a file or in command output.
  • wget: Downloads a file from a web address.
  • which: Prints the full path of the program a command name runs, or nothing when it is absent.
  • who: Lists who is signed in now, on which terminal, since when, and from where.
  • whoami: Prints the name of the account you are using right now.
  • xargs: Turns lines of input into arguments for another command, such as running a check on every file find lists.
  • xed: Opens a file in Xed, the Linux Mint graphical text editor.
  • xxd: Shows a file's bytes in hex beside their text, revealing its true file signature.
  • zcat: Prints the contents of a gzip-compressed file, such as an older rotated log like auth.log.2.gz.
  • zgrep: Searches compressed .gz files for matching lines the way grep searches plain text, such as older rotated logs like auth.log.2.gz.

FreeBSD

  • apachectl: Checks the Apache web server's configuration for mistakes and prints Syntax OK or the file and line with the error, so you catch errors before a restart.
  • atq: Lists jobs waiting in the at queue to run once at a later time, with job number, time, and owner; root sees every user's jobs.
  • awk: Splits each line of text into fields and prints or tests the ones you choose, such as finding accounts with UID 0 or an empty password field.
  • blocklistctl: Shows the addresses blocklistd tracks or blocks in pf after repeated failed sign-ins to sshd or other services; FreeBSD 14 and earlier name it blacklistctl.
  • boot: Starts FreeBSD from the boot loader prompt; boot -s opens single-user mode, a root shell before rc scripts start any services.
  • cap_mkdb: Rebuilds the login.conf database (/etc/login.conf.db), so edits to login classes, such as password aging and login retries, take effect.
  • cat: Prints the whole contents of one or more files to the screen, such as /etc/rc.conf, /etc/crontab, or the pkg repository files.
  • chflags: Sets or clears BSD file flags; schg (system immutable) blocks every change, even by root, so it is FreeBSD's version of Linux chattr.
  • chkrootkit: Scans the system for signs of known rootkits, worms, and hidden processes and prints anything suspicious; install it first with pkg install chkrootkit.
  • chmod: Changes who can read, write, or run a file, with numbers like 600 or letters like u-s, such as making /etc/master.passwd readable by root only.
  • chown: Changes the owner and group of files, such as making root and the wheel group own the password database files.
  • clamscan: Scans files and folders for known viruses and malware with ClamAV and lists the infected ones; install it with pkg install clamav.
  • crontab: Lists, edits, or removes a user's scheduled cron jobs; root can manage any user's table with -u. FreeBSD keeps these tables in /var/cron/tabs.
  • echo: Prints text; with >> it adds the text as a new last line of a file, such as a setting at the end of sshd_config.
  • file: Reads the start of a file and names what it really is, such as a shell script, an ELF program, or plain text, whatever its name suggests.
  • find: Searches folders for files that match tests, such as name, type, permissions, owner, or change date, and can run a command on each one.
  • for: Repeats commands once for each item in a list, such as running crontab -l for every account in /etc/passwd; type sh first if your shell is csh.
  • freebsd-update: Downloads and installs binary security patches for the FreeBSD base system and kernel, or upgrades to a new release; packages update separately with pkg.
  • freebsd-update fetch: Downloads the security and bug-fix patches for your FreeBSD release; adding install applies them to the base system and kernel.
  • freebsd-update IDS: Compares every base system file with the official SHA256 hashes for your release and lists files that differ, a built-in check for tampered system programs.
  • freebsd-version: Prints the FreeBSD release of the installed kernel, the running kernel, and the installed userland, which differ after a patch until you reboot.
  • freshclam: Downloads the newest ClamAV virus signatures so clamscan recognizes recent malware.
