  • grep: Searches files or command output for lines that match a word or pattern, such as NOPASSWD in sudoers or pam_permit in PAM files.
  • id: Shows a user's ID, main group, and every group they belong to, such as whether alice is in wheel.
  • ifconfig: Shows and sets network interfaces, such as em0 or vtnet0: addresses, up or down state, and hardware address; FreeBSD still uses it where Linux moved to ip.
  • kill: Sends a signal to a process by its PID: the default asks it to stop politely, and -9 ends it at once without cleanup.
  • last: Lists recent logins, logouts, reboots, and shutdowns, newest first, with user, terminal, source address, and time.
  • lastlogin: Shows each user's most recent login time, terminal, and source address, which reveals accounts that should not have signed in.
  • ls: Lists files and folders; -l adds permissions, owner, and size, and FreeBSD's -o adds file flags such as schg.
  • md5: Prints the MD5 fingerprint of a file, which changes if the file changes; FreeBSD's name for md5sum, which recent releases also accept.
  • passwd: Sets a new password for an account; anyone can change their own, and root can set any account's, including root's.
  • pfctl: Controls pf, the FreeBSD firewall: checks and loads the rules in /etc/pf.conf, turns filtering on or off, and shows rules, states, tables, and counters.
  • pkg: Installs, removes, updates, and checks third-party software packages under /usr/local; on a classic install the base system patches separately with freebsd-update.
  • pkg audit: Compares installed packages with the FreeBSD vulnerability database and lists the ones with known security holes; -F downloads the newest list first.
  • pkg autoremove: Removes packages that were installed only to support others and that nothing needs anymore.
  • pkg check: Checks installed packages; -s compares every package file's checksum with the package database, so a replaced binary such as sshd or ls shows up.
  • pkg delete: Uninstalls packages and the files they put under /usr/local, such as hacking tools or games the policy bans.
  • pkg info: Lists installed packages with their versions and short descriptions, or shows details and files for the packages you name.
  • pkg install: Downloads and installs a package and everything it needs from the configured repositories, such as rkhunter, clamav, or sudo.
  • pkg update: Downloads the latest package catalog from the repositories, so pkg knows which versions exist; it installs and changes nothing.
  • pkg upgrade: Upgrades installed packages to the newest versions in the catalog; pkg upgrade -r FreeBSD-base patches the base system on pkgbase installs (FreeBSD 15 and later).
  • pkg which: Names the package that installed a file, so you learn whether a program came from a package, the pkgbase base system, or nowhere known.
  • praudit: Prints OpenBSM audit trail files, such as /var/audit/current, as readable text: who logged in, used su, or ran programs.
  • procstat: Shows details of a running process; -b prints the full path of the program behind a PID, which exposes a backdoor hiding under an innocent name.
  • ps: Lists running processes with their process ID, parent, owner, and full command line, which exposes reverse shells and miners.
  • pw: Manages users and groups on FreeBSD in one tool; its subcommands useradd, usermod, userdel, usershow, lock, and groupmod replace Linux's separate useradd, usermod, and gpasswd.
  • pw groupmod: Changes a group, most often its members: -m adds users and -d removes them, such as taking a standard user out of wheel, the group allowed to su to root.
  • pw groupshow: Prints a group's line from /etc/group: name, group ID, and member list, such as who is in wheel or operator.
  • pw lock: Locks an account by putting *LOCKED* in front of its password hash, so nobody can sign in while its files stay for the investigation.
  • pw unlock: Unlocks an account that pw lock locked by removing *LOCKED* from its password hash, so its old password works again.
  • pw useradd: Creates a new user account; -m makes the home directory, -G adds extra groups, and -s picks the login shell.
  • pw userdel: Deletes a user account along with its mail spool, crontab, and at jobs; -r also removes the home directory and the files in it the user owns.
  • pw usermod: Changes an existing account, such as its shell, groups, login class, or password expiry; -s /usr/sbin/nologin stops a service account from logging in.
  • pw usershow: Prints an account's entry from the password database: UID, group, login class, expiry dates, home, and shell; -P labels each field, and root also sees the hash.
  • pwd_mkdb: Rebuilds /etc/pwd.db and /etc/spwd.db, and with -p also /etc/passwd, from /etc/master.passwd after a hand edit; vipw runs it for you.
  • rkhunter: Scans for rootkits, backdoors, and changed system programs by comparing files with a saved baseline; install it with pkg install rkhunter.
  • rm: Deletes files, or folders with -r, such as a planted script; there is no recycle bin, so the files are gone at once.
  • service: Starts, stops, restarts, and checks FreeBSD rc.d services; service X enable writes X_enable="YES" into /etc/rc.conf through sysrc, which is how FreeBSD starts it at boot.
  • sha256: Prints the SHA-256 fingerprint of a file, which changes if the file changes; FreeBSD's name for sha256sum, which recent releases also accept.
  • sockstat: Lists open network sockets with the user, program, and process ID behind each, such as what listens on port 22; FreeBSD's counterpart of Linux ss.
  • sshd: Checks the SSH server's configuration file with -t and prints any error, or nothing when the file is valid, so you catch errors before restarting sshd.
  • stat: Shows a file's details: owner, group, permissions, size, and the times it was last read, changed, and created.
  • strings: Prints the readable text inside a binary file, such as addresses, commands, or file paths, a quick look at what a suspicious program does.
  • sysctl: Reads or changes kernel settings while the system runs, such as kern.securelevel or net.inet.ip.forwarding; lines in /etc/sysctl.conf keep them after reboot.
  • sysrc: Reads, sets, or removes settings in /etc/rc.conf without opening an editor, such as sshd_enable=YES to start sshd at every boot; FreeBSD's counterpart of systemctl enable.
  • tail: Prints the last lines of a file, 10 unless you say otherwise, such as the newest entries in /var/log/auth.log; -f keeps watching for new lines.
  • tcpdump: Captures network packets on an interface and prints them; on pflog0 it shows the packets pf logged, such as blocked connection attempts.
  • uname: Prints system facts: the OS name, host name, release, kernel build, and hardware type.
  • vi: Opens a text file in the vi editor so you can change it, such as /etc/pf.conf, /etc/login.conf, or /etc/ssh/sshd_config.
  • vipw: Opens /etc/master.passwd in an editor with a lock, checks the file when you save, and rebuilds the password databases, the safe way to hand-edit accounts.
  • visudo: Edits the sudo rules in /usr/local/etc/sudoers with a lock and checks them before saving; on FreeBSD sudo is a package, so visudo exists only after pkg install sudo.
  • w: Shows who is logged in right now, from where, how long they have been idle, and what each is running, plus uptime and load.
  • which: Prints the full path of the program that runs when you type a command name, such as whether nc or socat is installed.

Cisco IOS

  • aaa authentication login: Sets how the device checks sign-ins; aaa authentication login default local makes every line ask for a username and password from the local accounts.
  • aaa new-model: Turns on the AAA system, which replaces the old per-line passwords with method lists for sign-in, such as local accounts or a RADIUS server.
  • access-class: Applies an access list to the VTY lines, so only the addresses it permits can open a Telnet or SSH session to the device.
  • access-list: Creates or adds a line to a numbered access list, a top-to-bottom list of permit and deny rules that filters traffic by address.
  • archive: Opens archive mode, where log config sets up a record of each configuration command and who typed it, and path saves dated copies of the configuration.
  • banner exec: Sets a message shown right after someone signs in and their session starts.
  • banner login: Sets a notice shown just before the username and password prompts, after the message of the day.
  • banner motd: Sets the message of the day, a notice shown to everyone who connects, before they sign in, such as a warning that access is monitored.
  • boot: Sets where the device loads its software or configuration at startup; no boot network stops it from loading a configuration from a network server.
  • cdp enable: Turns CDP on or off for one interface; no cdp enable keeps the device from announcing itself out that port, such as an ISP link.
  • cdp run: Turns the Cisco Discovery Protocol on or off for the whole device; no cdp run stops it from telling neighbors its model, IOS version, and addresses.
  • cdp timer: Sets how often, in seconds, the device sends CDP announcements to its neighbors; the default is 60.
  • clear ip ospf process: Restarts OSPF on the router, so new settings such as a router-id take effect and neighbors form again.
  • clear line: Disconnects whoever is using a console or VTY line, ending their session.
  • clear mac address-table: Empties the switch's learned MAC address table, so it relearns which device sits on which port.
  • clear port-security: Removes secure MAC addresses that port security learned, such as an old sticky address after a device is replaced.
  • clock set: Sets the device's date and time by hand, which makes log timestamps match real time.
  • clock summer-time: Turns on daylight saving time for the clock, such as clock summer-time PDT recurring.
  • clock timezone: Sets the time zone name and its offset from UTC, so the clock and log timestamps show local time.
  • config-register: Sets the configuration register, the boot setting that decides whether the router loads its saved configuration at the next reload.
  • configure terminal: Enters global configuration mode, where you type the settings that change how the device works.
  • connect: Opens a Telnet session to another device, the same as the telnet command.
  • copy flash:: Copies a file from flash memory to another place, such as an IOS image to a TFTP server for backup.
  • copy running-config: Saves a backup copy of the running configuration to a file in flash or on a TFTP server.
  • copy running-config startup-config: Saves the running configuration to NVRAM as the startup configuration, so your changes survive a reload or power loss.
  • copy startup-config running-config: Merges the saved startup configuration into the running configuration, bringing back saved lines while keeping lines added since.
  • copy tftp:: Copies a file from a TFTP server onto the device, such as a new IOS image into flash or a configuration file.
  • crypto key generate rsa: Makes the RSA key pair that the SSH server needs; set a hostname and ip domain-name first, because the key is named after them.
  • crypto key zeroize rsa: Deletes the device's RSA key pairs, which also turns the SSH server off.
  • debug: Prints live details of what a feature is doing, such as debug ip ospf adjacency, for troubleshooting.
  • default-information originate: Advertises this router's default route to its OSPF neighbors, so they send Internet-bound traffic here.
  • default-router: Sets the default gateway that this DHCP pool gives to its clients.
  • delete: Deletes a file from flash memory or another file system on the device.
  • deny: Adds a block line to the access list you are editing; the first line a packet matches decides what happens to it.
  • description: Labels an interface with a note, such as Trunk to SwA G0/1, so admins know what each port connects to.
  • dir: Lists the files in flash memory or NVRAM, such as the IOS image and saved configurations, with their sizes.
  • disable: Leaves privileged EXEC and returns to user EXEC, the > prompt with read-only commands.
  • dns-server: Sets the DNS server address that this DHCP pool gives to its clients.
  • do: Runs an EXEC command, such as a show command or a save, without leaving configuration mode.
  • domain-name: Sets the domain name that this DHCP pool gives to its clients.
  • duplex: Sets whether a port sends and receives at the same time (full), takes turns (half), or works it out with the other end (auto).
  • enable: Moves from user EXEC (>) to privileged EXEC (#), asking for the enable secret if one is set.
  • enable algorithm-type: Sets the enable secret with a stronger hash than the default type 5, such as scrypt (type 9) or PBKDF2 with SHA-256 (type 8).
  • enable password: Sets the old-style privileged EXEC password, stored in plain text or weak type 7; use enable secret and remove this one.
  • enable secret: Sets the password for privileged EXEC (#), stored as a one-way hash (type 5, MD5, by default on IOS 15); it wins over enable password when both exist.
  • encapsulation dot1q: Tags a router subinterface with one VLAN, so it becomes that VLAN's gateway on a router-on-a-stick trunk.
  • end: Leaves any configuration mode and returns straight to privileged EXEC; Ctrl+Z does the same.
  • erase startup-config: Deletes the saved startup configuration from NVRAM, so the device starts with a blank configuration at the next reload.
  • errdisable recovery: Brings err-disabled ports back up on their own after a wait, such as ports shut by port security or BPDU guard.
  • exec: Controls whether a line can start a CLI session; no exec closes an unused port such as aux to anyone who plugs in.
  • exec-banner: Controls whether this line shows the EXEC and message-of-the-day banners; no exec-banner hides both on that line.
  • exec-timeout: Signs out an idle session on the line after the time you set, so an unattended console or SSH window closes itself.
  • exit: Goes back one level, such as from interface configuration to global configuration, or signs out when typed at the EXEC prompt.
  • help: Explains how the built-in help works; typing ? after a word lists what can come next.
  • hidekeys: Hides passwords and keys in the configuration change log and its log messages, so the record of changes leaks no secrets.
  • history size: Sets how many recent commands this line remembers for the up-arrow and show history; the default is 10.
  • hostname: Gives the device its name, which shows in the prompt and is needed before making RSA keys for SSH.
  • interface: Selects one interface to configure, such as a port, a VLAN interface (SVI), or a router subinterface.
  • interface range: Selects several interfaces at once, so one set of commands configures them all, such as shutting every unused port.
  • ip access-group: Applies an access list to an interface, filtering the packets that arrive (in) or leave (out) through that port.
  • ip access-list extended: Creates or opens a named extended access list, which filters by protocol, source, destination, and port, such as an inbound edge list.
  • ip access-list standard: Creates or opens a named or numbered standard access list, which filters by source address, and lets you add, insert, or remove single lines.
  • ip address: Gives an interface, SVI, or subinterface its IPv4 address and subnet mask.
  • ip arp inspection: Turns on Dynamic ARP Inspection for a VLAN, which drops ARP packets that disagree with the DHCP snooping records, stopping ARP poisoning.
  • ip arp inspection trust: Marks a port as trusted for Dynamic ARP Inspection, such as an uplink, so its ARP traffic passes unchecked.
  • ip bootp server: Turns the BOOTP server on or off; no ip bootp server closes an old address-assignment service that few networks need.
  • ip classless: Lets the router use its default route for unknown subnets of networks it partly knows; it is on by default.
  • ip default-gateway: Sets the router a layer 2 switch sends its own management traffic through, so you can reach the switch from other subnets.
  • ip dhcp excluded-address: Reserves addresses for the DHCP server to skip, such as the gateway and printers.
  • ip dhcp pool: Creates a DHCP address pool on the router, so it hands out addresses, a gateway, and DNS settings to clients.
  • ip dhcp snooping: Turns on DHCP snooping, which drops DHCP server replies from untrusted ports so only the trusted DHCP server hands out addresses.
  • ip dhcp snooping limit rate: Limits how many DHCP packets per second a port may send; a port over the limit is shut down (err-disabled).
  • ip dhcp snooping trust: Marks a port as trusted for DHCP snooping, such as the uplink toward the real DHCP server, so its DHCP replies pass.
  • ip dhcp snooping vlan: Chooses the VLANs where DHCP snooping watches for rogue DHCP servers.
  • ip directed-broadcast: Controls whether a packet sent to a whole subnet's broadcast address is passed on; no ip directed-broadcast blocks smurf attacks.
  • ip domain lookup: Controls DNS lookups of names, the newer spelling of ip domain-lookup; no ip domain lookup stops typos from being looked up as hostnames.
  • ip domain name: Sets the device's default DNS domain name, the newer spelling of ip domain-name.
  • ip domain-lookup: Controls DNS lookups of names; no ip domain-lookup stops a mistyped command from freezing the prompt while it is looked up as a hostname.
  • ip domain-name: Sets the device's default DNS domain name, such as school.lan; SSH setup needs it because the RSA key is named hostname.domain.
  • ip finger: Turns the finger service on or off; no ip finger stops the device from telling anyone who asks which users are signed in.
  • ip helper-address: Forwards DHCP requests that arrive on this interface to a DHCP server in another subnet, so clients there still get addresses.
  • ip http authentication: Sets how the web management page checks sign-ins, such as with the local accounts or the enable password.
  • ip http port: Changes a web management server setting, such as ip http port 8080, which moves the HTTP page to a different port.
  • ip http secure-server: Turns the HTTPS web management page on or off; no ip http secure-server closes it when nobody manages the device from a browser.
  • ip http server: Turns the plain-HTTP web management page on or off; no ip http server closes that unencrypted way in.
  • ip mask-reply: Controls whether the interface answers ICMP requests for its subnet mask; no ip mask-reply keeps the answer to itself.
  • ip name-server: Sets the DNS server the device asks when it turns hostnames into addresses.
  • ip proxy-arp: Controls whether the router answers ARP requests for addresses on other networks; no ip proxy-arp turns that off.
  • ip redirects: Controls whether the interface sends ICMP redirect messages; no ip redirects stops them, which hides routing details.
  • ip route: Adds a static route that tells the router where to send traffic for a network, through a next-hop address or an exit interface.
  • ip routing: Turns on routing between networks; routers have it on already, and layer 3 switches need it to route between VLANs.
  • ip source-route: Controls whether the router honors packets that pick their own path; no ip source-route drops them, closing a spoofing trick.
  • ip ssh authentication-retries: Sets how many password tries an SSH connection gets before the device closes it.
  • ip ssh time-out: Sets how many seconds a person has to finish signing in over SSH before the connection closes.
  • ip ssh version: Sets which SSH version the server accepts; ip ssh version 2 turns off the weaker version 1.
  • ip unreachables: Controls whether the interface sends ICMP unreachable messages; no ip unreachables stops them, which slows network mapping.
  • ipv6: Sets a device-wide IPv6 option; the one met first, ipv6 unicast-routing, lets a router forward IPv6 packets between its interfaces.
  • line aux: Opens the settings for the auxiliary port, a router port meant for a modem that can open a CLI session.
  • line console: Opens the settings for the console port, the cable connection right on the device, such as its password and time-out.
  • line vty: Opens the settings for the virtual terminal lines that Telnet and SSH sessions use, such as passwords, transport, and access lists.
  • lldp receive: Lets this port read LLDP announcements from the device on the other end; no lldp receive makes the port ignore them.
  • lldp run: Turns the standard Link Layer Discovery Protocol on or off for the whole device; no lldp run stops it from announcing itself to neighbors.
  • lldp transmit: Lets this port send LLDP announcements about the switch; no lldp transmit keeps the switch's name, model, and address off that port.
  • log config: Opens the configuration change log settings inside archive mode, where logging enable starts recording each configuration command and the user who typed it.
  • log-adjacency-changes: Logs a message each time an OSPF neighbor comes up or goes down; it is on by default.
  • logging buffered: Keeps recent log messages in the device's memory, where show logging can display them.
  • logging console: Sets which log messages print on the console; no logging console stops them from interrupting console work.
  • logging enable: Starts the configuration change log, which records every command typed in configuration mode along with the user who typed it.
  • logging host: Sends the device's log messages to a syslog server, so a copy survives even if the device is wiped or restarted.
  • logging synchronous: Reprints your half-typed command after a log message interrupts it, so messages stop scrambling what you type.
  • logging trap: Sets the lowest severity of messages sent to the syslog server, such as informational or warnings.
  • login: Turns on the password check for a line; login local asks for a username and password from the local accounts instead.
  • login block-for: Blocks remote sign-ins (Telnet, SSH, and HTTP) for a while after too many failures in a short time, which slows password guessing; the console still works.
  • login on-failure: Writes a log message each time a sign-in fails, so password guessing shows up in the logs.
  • login on-success: Writes a log message each time someone signs in successfully, so you have a record of who connected.
  • logout: Ends your session on the device and signs you out.
  • mdix auto: Lets a switch port detect the cable type and swap its send and receive pairs, so straight-through and crossover cables both work.
  • monitor session: Sets up a SPAN session that copies traffic from ports or a VLAN to another port, where a capture tool such as tcpdump can watch it.
  • motd-banner: Controls whether this line shows the message-of-the-day banner; no motd-banner hides it on that line.
  • name: Names the VLAN you are configuring, such as STUDENTS, so show vlan lists something meaningful.
  • network: Under router ospf, turns on OSPF for interfaces in an address range and assigns their area; in a DHCP pool, sets the subnet handed out.
  • no <sequence>: Removes one line from an access list by its sequence number, the number shown beside each line in show access-lists.
  • ntp authenticate: Turns on NTP authentication, so the device accepts time only from servers that prove a shared key.
  • ntp master: Makes this device an NTP time source for others, using its own clock at the stratum you give.
  • ntp server: Tells the device to get its time from an NTP server, so its clock and log timestamps stay accurate and match the rest of the network.
  • passive-interface: Stops OSPF from sending hellos out an interface, such as a LAN with only PCs, while still advertising that network.
  • password: Sets the password for the console or VTY lines you are configuring; login makes the line ask for it.
  • permit: Adds an allow line to the access list you are editing; the first line a packet matches decides what happens to it.
  • ping: Sends test packets to an address and reports how many replies came back, which shows whether the path works.
  • privilege: Sets the privilege level that sessions on this line start at, such as level 15 for full control right after sign-in.
  • redistribute: Shares routes from another source, such as static routes, with OSPF neighbors.
  • reload: Restarts the device, which loads the startup configuration and drops every session.
  • remark: Adds a comment line to the access list you are editing, so the next admin knows what the list is for.
  • router bgp: Starts BGP, the routing protocol that links networks run by different organizations, for an autonomous system number.
  • router eigrp: Starts EIGRP, Cisco's advanced distance-vector routing protocol, for an autonomous system number, and opens its settings.
  • router ospf: Starts an OSPF process and opens its settings, where network commands choose which interfaces share routes.
  • router rip: Starts RIP, an older routing protocol that counts hops, and opens its settings.
  • router-id: Sets the OSPF router ID, the address-style name each router uses with its neighbors; if OSPF already chose an ID, the new one applies after clear ip ospf process.
  • secure boot-image / boot-config: Turns on resilient configuration, which keeps a hidden, protected copy of the IOS image and the running configuration that erase and delete commands leave intact.
  • security passwords min-length: Sets the shortest password the device accepts for new enable, line, and user passwords.
  • send: Sends a text message to users on other lines, such as a warning before a reload.
  • service config: Controls whether the device loads its configuration from a network server at startup; no service config keeps it on the saved configuration.
  • service pad: Turns the old X.25 packet assembler service on or off; no service pad closes a service modern networks leave unused.
  • service password-encryption: Hides plain-text passwords in the configuration with type 7 encoding, which stops someone reading over your shoulder but free tools decode in seconds.
  • service password-recovery: Controls the password-recovery break sequence at startup; no service password-recovery stops someone with the console cable from bypassing the passwords.
  • service tcp-keepalives-in: Checks incoming TCP sessions, such as VTY logins, for a live other end and closes dead ones, which frees their lines.
  • service tcp-keepalives-out: Checks outgoing TCP sessions started from the device for a live other end and closes dead ones.
  • service tcp-small-servers: Turns the small TCP test services, such as echo, discard, and chargen, on or off; no service tcp-small-servers closes them.
  • service timestamps: Adds the date and time (down to the millisecond with msec) to each log or debug message, so events line up with other logs.
  • service udp-small-servers: Turns the small UDP test services, such as echo, discard, and chargen, on or off; no service udp-small-servers closes them.
  • session-timeout: Closes a connection opened from this line to another device after it sits idle for the given number of minutes.
  • setup: Starts a question-and-answer dialog that builds a basic configuration, such as hostname, passwords, and interface addresses.
  • show access-lists: Lists every access list with its numbered lines and a count of the packets each line has matched.
  • show arp: Lists the ARP table, which pairs each IP address the device has talked to with its MAC address.
  • show cdp: Shows whether CDP is running on the device, with how often it announces itself and how long neighbors keep its details.
  • show cdp neighbors: Lists the Cisco devices directly connected to this one, learned through CDP: their names, models, and the ports that link you.
  • show clock: Shows the device's current date, time, and time zone; a leading * or . means the clock is unsynced.
  • show crypto key mypubkey rsa: Shows the device's RSA public keys, which proves the key pair SSH needs exists.
  • show flash: Lists the files in flash memory, such as the IOS image, and shows how much space is free.
  • show history: Lists the commands you typed recently in this session.
  • show interfaces: Shows each interface's status, hardware address, speed, duplex, and error counters, such as input errors and collisions.
  • show interfaces description: Lists each interface with its status and the description label it was given.
  • show interfaces status: Lists every switch port on one line with its label, state (connected, notconnect, err-disabled), VLAN, duplex, and speed.
  • show interfaces switchport: Shows each switch port's mode (access or trunk), its access VLAN, native VLAN, and whether it negotiates trunking.
  • show interfaces trunk: Lists the trunk ports with their native VLAN and the VLANs each one allows and carries.
  • show ip access-lists: Lists the IPv4 access lists with their lines and match counts, the same view as show access-lists limited to IP lists.
  • show ip arp: Lists the IPv4 ARP table, pairing each IP address with its MAC address and interface.
  • show ip dhcp binding: Lists the addresses the router's DHCP server has handed out, with each client's hardware address and lease time.
  • show ip dhcp snooping: Shows whether DHCP snooping is on, which VLANs it watches, and which ports are trusted.
  • show ip interface: Shows each interface's IP address and status; show ip interface brief fits every interface on one line each.
  • show ip ospf: Shows OSPF process details, such as the router ID, areas, and timers.
  • show ip ospf interface: Shows which interfaces run OSPF, their area, cost, and neighbor count.
  • show ip ospf neighbor: Lists OSPF neighbors with their router ID, state, and interface; FULL means the two routers have finished swapping their route databases.
  • show ip protocols: Shows which routing protocols run, the networks each advertises, its passive interfaces, and where routes come from.
  • show ip route: Shows the routing table: every network the router knows, how it learned each one, and where it sends that traffic.
  • show ip ssh: Shows whether the SSH server is on, its version, time-out, and retry limit.
  • show line: Lists every console, aux, and VTY line with its status, speed, and settings.
  • show lldp neighbors: Lists the devices directly connected to this one that announce themselves with LLDP, the open standard that devices from any vendor can speak.
  • show logging: Shows the logging settings and the recent log messages kept in memory, such as interface changes and failed sign-ins.
  • show login: Shows the sign-in protection settings, such as login block-for, and whether the device is blocking sign-ins right now.
  • show mac address-table: Lists the MAC addresses the switch has learned and the port and VLAN where each device sits.
  • show ntp associations: Lists the NTP servers the device talks to and marks the one it is synced with, with an asterisk.
  • show ntp status: Shows whether the clock is synchronized through NTP, its stratum, and the server it follows.
  • show port-security: Shows port security on each port: the address limit, the addresses learned, violation counts, and the action taken.
  • show privilege: Shows the privilege level of your current session, such as 1 for user EXEC or 15 for full control.
  • show running-config: Shows the configuration the device is using right now, including changes typed since the last save.
  • show sessions: Lists the Telnet and SSH connections you opened from this device to others, so you can resume or close them.
  • show spanning-tree: Shows the spanning tree for each VLAN: which switch is the root, and whether each port is forwarding or blocking.
  • show ssh: Lists the SSH sessions connected to this device right now, with their users and encryption.
  • show startup-config: Shows the saved configuration in NVRAM, the one the device loads at the next reload.
  • show tech-support: Prints a very long report that bundles the configuration, version, interfaces, and logs, usually saved for a support ticket.
  • show users: Lists who is signed in on each line, console or VTY, and where they connected from; an asterisk marks your own session.
  • show version: Shows the IOS version, model, uptime, memory, serial number, and the reason for the last restart.
  • show vlan: Lists the VLANs on the switch with their names, status, and the access ports in each.
  • show vtp status: Shows the switch's VTP mode, domain name, and configuration revision number.
  • shutdown: Turns an interface off; no shutdown turns it on, which router interfaces need because they start off.
  • snmp-server: Sets up the SNMP agent that monitoring systems poll; no snmp-server turns SNMP off completely.
  • snmp-server community: Sets an SNMP v1/v2c community string, a shared password that lets monitoring tools read (RO) or change (RW) the device's settings.
  • snmp-server group: Creates an SNMPv3 group and sets its security level, such as priv, which requires both message authentication and encryption.
  • snmp-server user: Creates an SNMPv3 user in a group, with an authentication password and an encryption password.
  • spanning-tree bpdufilter: Stops a port from sending or receiving spanning tree messages, which takes the port out of loop protection.
  • spanning-tree bpduguard: Shuts a port (err-disabled) the moment it hears from another switch, which keeps a rogue or misplaced switch out of the spanning tree.
  • spanning-tree cost: Sets the spanning tree cost of a port, which changes which path spanning tree keeps open; lower cost is preferred.
  • spanning-tree extend system-id: Changes a global spanning tree setting; spanning-tree extend system-id, on by default, adds the VLAN number to each bridge ID.
  • spanning-tree guard: Turns on root guard or loop guard for a port, so it refuses to let a device there become the root bridge or form a loop.
  • spanning-tree mode: Picks the spanning tree version the switch runs, such as rapid-pvst, which recovers from link changes in seconds.
  • spanning-tree portfast: Lets an access port start forwarding as soon as a device plugs in, skipping the spanning tree wait of about 30 seconds.
  • spanning-tree vlan: Tunes spanning tree for a VLAN, such as making this switch the root bridge with root primary or a lower priority.
  • speed: Sets a port's speed in megabits per second or lets it negotiate with the other end.
  • ssh: Opens an encrypted SSH session from this device to another device, signing in as the user you name.
  • state: Sets a VLAN to active or suspend; a suspended VLAN passes no traffic.
  • storm-control: Limits broadcast, multicast, or unicast traffic on a port to a share of its bandwidth, which contains broadcast storms.
  • switchport: Sets a port's switching features; switchport protected keeps protected ports from talking to each other, and no switchport makes a routed port on layer 3 switches.
  • switchport access vlan: Puts an access port into a VLAN, so the device plugged in joins that network; the switch creates the VLAN if it is missing.
  • switchport mode: Sets a switch port as an access port in one VLAN, a trunk that carries many VLANs, or a port that negotiates with DTP.
  • switchport nonegotiate: Turns off DTP on a port set to access or trunk, so it keeps that mode whatever is plugged in, which blocks switch-spoofing attacks.
  • switchport port-security: Turns on port security, which limits an access port to known MAC addresses and acts when an unknown device plugs in; set switchport mode access first.
  • switchport trunk allowed vlan: Sets which VLANs a trunk carries, so only the VLANs that belong on that link cross it.
  • switchport trunk encapsulation: Picks the trunk tagging type on switches that also support ISL, such as the 3560; it comes before switchport mode trunk.
  • switchport trunk native vlan: Sets the native VLAN, the one a trunk carries untagged; both ends must match, and an unused VLAN such as 99 blocks double-tagging attacks.
  • switchport voice vlan: Sets a second VLAN for an IP phone on an access port, so phone traffic is tagged apart from the PC's data VLAN.
  • telnet: Opens a Telnet session from this device to another device; everything, passwords included, travels unencrypted.
  • terminal length: Sets how many lines of output show before --More-- pauses; terminal length 0 prints long output without pausing.
  • terminal monitor: Shows log and debug messages in your SSH or Telnet session, which by default only the console sees.
  • terminal no monitor: Stops showing log and debug messages in your SSH or Telnet session.
  • traceroute: Lists each router a packet passes through on the way to an address, which shows where a path breaks.
  • transport input: Sets which protocols can open a session on these lines; transport input ssh allows SSH and refuses Telnet, which sends passwords in clear text.
  • transport output: Sets which protocols a user on these lines can use to connect onward to other devices, such as transport output ssh.
  • transport preferred: Sets the protocol the line assumes when you type only a hostname; transport preferred none stops typos from turning into connection attempts.
  • undebug all: Turns off every running debug at once.
  • username: Creates or changes a local account that can sign in with login local, with its password and privilege level; no username deletes it.
  • vlan: Creates a VLAN, or opens it to name it, so ports can be grouped into separate networks on one switch.
  • vtp: Sets a VLAN Trunking Protocol setting, such as vtp domain, which names the group of switches that share VLAN lists.
  • vtp mode: Sets how the switch takes part in VTP; transparent keeps its own VLAN list and ignores updates from other switches.
  • where: Lists the connections you opened from this device to others, the same as show sessions.
  • write: Saves the running configuration to NVRAM; write by itself does the same as write memory.
  • write memory: Saves the running configuration as the startup configuration, the short form of copy running-config startup-config.

Every practice place was confirmed in its app when this map was built. Apps as of 2026-10-26.
